name: Dasyatis plicata
note: A speculative field note written by Claude. The species is invented; the natural history of every part it is made from is real.
lineage: The paper ray is folded from animals that solved floating, gliding and hiding long before rays existed. Down its spine sit two cephalopods: the chambered nautilus, whose line goes back about 500 million years and which still rises and sinks by trimming gas in its shell, and the argonaut, an octopus whose female makes a paper-thin shell to carry her eggs. Its fin rays are the wings of dragonflies and damselflies, among them Epiophlebia, a relict from Japanese mountain streams that is neither dragonfly nor damselfly but the survivor of a group that flew in the Jurassic. Between those ancient lines the ray is stitched together with leaf skeletons, single-celled shell-builders and a water bear, as if a lineage had been pressed flat between the pages of every other one.
habitat: Warm, clear shallows over sand made largely of the shells of foraminifera, the same single-celled builders whose chambered shell lines its belly. Its underside carries a water bear, so the paper ray is at home where pools dry out and return: when a lagoon drains at low tide it can lie still under a skin of damp sand and wait. It keeps to water clean enough for beard lichen to hang from the mangrove roots above it, and the pale shells of its back are hard to tell from the seabed it settles on.
behaviour: It swims the way real stingrays do: not by beating its fins but by sending a wave back along the edge of its disc, so the dragonfly wings of its margin ripple one after another while the whip tail trails and steers. When it settles, the wave slows to a breath, the disc flattens against the sand, and only the two abalone lobes at its snout stay raised. Its barb is a velvet worm, and it defends itself the way that animal hunts: not with venom but with a sudden thread of glue, fired at whatever comes too close.

wm-965622.fact: A dragonfly wing: a thin membrane braced by a network of veins. Dragonflies can move each of their four wings independently.

wm-38227268.fact: The wings of a male flatwing damselfly from Australia. Flatwings rest with their wings held open rather than folded over the back.

wm-38227267.fact: The wings of a female flatwing damselfly, the mirror of the male's along the ray's edge.

wm-97530111.fact: A skeleton leaf: what remains when the soft tissue rots or is eaten away, leaving only the veins that carried water and sugar.

wm-95636803.fact: Dragonfly wings, photographed in a terrace garden. The dark cell near each wing tip, the pterostigma, adds weight there and steadies the wing in flight.

wm-9054150.fact: Epiophlebia superstes, a relict odonate from Japanese mountain streams: neither dragonfly nor damselfly, but the survivor of a group that was widespread in the Jurassic.

wm-176863941.fact: A leaf left in pond water until only its veins remained: the slow work of bacteria and fungi.

wm-22949237.fact: The vein skeleton of a thistle leaf, found in the Dutch dunes; even the spines at its edge are kept as veins.

wm-52411719.fact: Malachite from the Urals: a copper carbonate that grows in concentric green bands. Ural malachite panelled whole rooms of Russian palaces.

inat-102249138.fact: The greater argonaut, or paper nautilus, is an octopus, not a nautilus. The female secretes this paper-thin shell as a case for her eggs.

wm-70143157.fact: A pollen grain under the scanning electron microscope. Pollen walls are so durable and so particular to each plant that fossil pollen can identify ancient vegetation.

wm-143637764.fact: A foraminifer: a single-celled organism that builds a chambered shell. Their shells pile up into chalk, limestone and whole beaches of sand.

wm-133169066.fact: A conch pearl, from the queen conch. It has no nacre; its sheen is a flame-like pattern of crystals, and almost all are found by chance rather than farmed.

wm-17579839.fact: An abalone with a conical pearl. Abalone pearls are rarely round; they tend to grow as horns and cones following the spiral of the shell.

wm-189902967.fact: Dragonfly wings. Each is corrugated like folded paper, which makes a very light wing surprisingly stiff.

inat-6251325.fact: Another argonaut shell. A floating female traps a bubble of air in it to stay level in the water.

inat-185657952.fact: A giant thorny oyster. It cements itself to rock and grows long spines that algae and sponges settle on, so it disappears into the reef.

wm-2604772.fact: Nacre, or mother-of-pearl: tiles of aragonite bonded by protein. The layering makes it iridescent and far tougher than the mineral alone.

inat-470639183.fact: The chambered nautilus rises and sinks by moving gas and fluid through the chambers of its shell. Its lineage is around 500 million years old.

inat-457452570.fact: A water bear, a tardigrade half a millimetre long. Dried out, it can survive for years in suspended animation and revive in water.

wm-17579893.fact: An abalone blister pearl, grown fixed to the inside of the shell, often where the animal walled off an intruder.

inat-406673799.fact: The greater lophorina, a bird-of-paradise. The male's display cape is made of feathers so black that they absorb almost all light.

inat-450700972.fact: The Queen Victoria agave, a slow Mexican succulent edged with white lines. It may grow for decades before it flowers once and dies.

wm-118496726.fact: The round-leaved sundew. Each tentacle ends in a drop of sticky mucilage that catches insects; the leaf then curls around them to digest them.

inat-288010505.fact: The Asian arowana, a bony-tongued fish of a very old lineage. Males carry the eggs and young in their mouths.

inat-40009588.fact: Methuselah's beard lichen hangs in strands that can grow several metres long, and only where the air is clean and humid.

inat-226306189.fact: A velvet worm from New Zealand. It hunts by squirting threads of sticky slime from glands beside its mouth, pinning its prey in place.
